overview: This two-page file consists of a “List of Papers” indexing fifteen numbered records, plus related Department telegrams, concerning military affairs in the Kwantung Leased Territory and Manchuria from 1935 through at least 1938. Much of the list concerns air-defense exercises at Dairen and official efforts to obtain financial contributions from foreign firms, which prompted U.S. diplomatic representations based on the 1911 treaty with Japan. Later entries address the Kwantung Army’s relations with the Manchukuo government, the South Manchuria Railway Company, and the Japanese War Ministry, as well as military preparations and reported changes within the army. The underlying telegrams, despatches, letters, and enclosures are indexed but are not reproduced in the supplied text.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Military Affairs—Kwantung
subfiles.about: A two-page index summarizes fifteen records concerning Dairen air defense and the activities and institutional relationships of the Kwantung Army.
subfiles.summary: The first portion indexes 1935 reports and telegrams about air-defense maneuvers in the Kwantung Leased Territory and requests by the mayor of Dairen that foreign firms help finance local air defense. It records U.S. concern about possible coercion, business retaliation, and infringement of the 1911 treaty with Japan, followed by assurances that the Japanese government disapproved of the mayor’s action. The continuation lists later material on Dairen air-defense practice, the Kwantung Army’s relations with the Manchukuo government and the South Manchuria Railway Company, disagreement with the Tokyo War Ministry, military preparations in Manchuria, current army activities, and rumors of changes within the Kwantung Army.

interest: The index is useful for reconstructing a dispersed documentary sequence even though the underlying papers are absent. Its most revealing episode is the attempt to enlist foreign businesses in Dairen’s air-defense program and the U.S. effort to distinguish indirect pressure and feared commercial retaliation from overt legal compulsion. The later entries offer a compact research guide to tensions among the Kwantung Army, Manchukuo authorities, the South Manchuria Railway Company, and ministries in Tokyo, illuminating the army’s semi-autonomous position in Japanese-controlled Manchuria.
